subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Meeting the specification and user needs

questions.q: What is the main purpose of testing a prototype during product development?
options: To increase the selling price of the product
To check whether the design works and meets requirements
To register the design for a patent
To advertise the product to potential customers
questions.explain: Testing a prototype allows a designer to gather evidence about whether the design functions correctly and satisfies its requirements.

questions.q: Gathering the opinions of intended users when evaluating a prototype is an example of which type of feedback?
options: Qualitative feedback
Financial forecasting
Automated testing
Copyright checking
questions.explain: Users' opinions and comments are descriptive, non-numerical data, which is known as qualitative feedback.

questions.q: Why is objective testing (such as measuring dimensions or loads) often more reliable than relying only on the designer's own opinion?
options: It always costs less money to carry out
It removes personal bias and gives measurable evidence
It guarantees the product will sell well
It means user feedback is no longer needed
questions.explain: Objective testing produces measurable, repeatable data that is not influenced by the designer's personal preferences.

questions.q: A designer builds a working model to check that moving parts fit and operate correctly before manufacture. What is this an example of?
options: Market segmentation
Prototyping and testing
Planned obsolescence
Life cycle assessment
questions.explain: Making a working model to check function and fit before full production is prototyping and testing.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes an iterative approach to designing and evaluating?
options: Producing one final design with no changes
Repeatedly testing, evaluating and improving a design
Copying an existing product exactly
Only evaluating the product after it has been sold
questions.explain: An iterative approach involves repeated cycles of testing, evaluating and refining to improve the design.

questions.q: A student tests a phone stand and records that it topples when a phone is placed on it. What is the most appropriate next step in the design process?
options: Put the product straight into mass production
Modify the design to improve stability and retest
Ignore the result as it is only one test
Increase the retail price to cover the fault
questions.explain: Test results showing a fault should lead to modification and further testing to resolve the problem.

questions.q: A company wants unbiased data on how long a hinge lasts before failing. Which testing method is most suitable?
options: Asking the designer for their opinion
Repeated mechanical cycling of the hinge until it fails
Checking the product's brand reputation
Looking at the colour of the material
questions.explain: Cycling the hinge repeatedly until failure gives measurable, objective data on its durability.

questions.q: What is a design specification?
options: A list of criteria a product must meet
A drawing of the final product only
A record of the company's yearly profits
A schedule for advertising the product
questions.explain: A design specification is a set of criteria or requirements that a product must satisfy.

questions.q: In specification writing, requirements are often sorted into 'needs' and 'wants'. What does a 'need' represent?
options: A desirable but optional feature
An essential requirement the product must meet
A feature added only to raise the price
A marketing slogan for the product
questions.explain: A 'need' is an essential, must-have requirement, whereas a 'want' is desirable but not essential.

questions.q: Why is it important to check a design against each point of its specification?
options: To confirm the product meets all stated requirements
To increase the number of components used
To avoid having to test the product
To guarantee the lowest possible material cost
questions.explain: Checking the design against the specification confirms whether every requirement has been met.

questions.q: A specification states a children's toy must have 'no small detachable parts'. This criterion is mainly intended to address which user need?
options: Aesthetics
Safety
Cost
Sustainability
questions.explain: Preventing small detachable parts reduces choking hazards, addressing the user's safety needs.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why a specification should be measurable where possible?
options: It makes the product cheaper automatically
It allows the finished product to be tested objectively against the criteria
It removes the need for user feedback
It ensures the product cannot be copied
questions.explain: Measurable criteria (for example a maximum mass) let designers test objectively whether the product meets them.

questions.q: A specification requires a lamp to weigh no more than 500 g. A prototype weighs 620 g. What does this evaluation tell the designer?
options: The lamp fully meets the specification
The lamp fails this criterion and must be modified
The specification should be ignored
The lamp is ready to be sold
questions.explain: At 620 g the lamp exceeds the 500 g limit, so it fails the criterion and requires modification.

questions.q: What does 'commercial viability' of a design mean?
options: Whether the product can be made and sold at a profit
Whether the product looks attractive
Whether the product can be recycled
Whether the product is easy to draw
questions.explain: Commercial viability concerns whether a product can be produced and sold profitably in the market.

questions.q: Which tool is used to assess the environmental impact of a product across its whole life, from raw materials to disposal?
options: Life cycle assessment
Gantt chart
Bill of materials
Orthographic drawing
questions.explain: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates a product's environmental impact from raw material extraction through to disposal.

questions.q: Why might designing a product so that its parts can be easily separated improve its environmental viability?
options: It makes the product more expensive to buy
It makes recycling of the materials easier at end of life
It reduces the number of tests needed
It guarantees higher sales
questions.explain: Products designed for disassembly allow materials to be separated and recycled more easily, reducing waste.

questions.q: How can the choice of manufacturing scale (for example one-off versus mass production) affect the commercial viability of a design?
options: Scale has no effect on unit cost
Higher production volumes usually reduce the cost per unit
One-off production is always the cheapest per unit
Mass production always increases the cost per unit
questions.explain: Economies of scale mean that higher production volumes typically lower the cost per unit, improving commercial viability.

questions.q: Which of the following would most reduce the environmental impact of a product?
options: Using more virgin, non-renewable materials
Selecting recycled or renewable materials
Increasing the amount of packaging
Designing the product to fail quickly
questions.explain: Choosing recycled or renewable materials lowers demand on finite resources and reduces environmental impact.

questions.q: A designer must decide between two materials: one is cheaper but non-recyclable, the other slightly more expensive but recyclable. To balance commercial and environmental viability, what should they consider?
options: Only the purchase cost of the material
The trade-off between cost and environmental impact over the product's life
Only the colour of each material
Whichever material is quicker to draw
questions.explain: Balancing viability requires weighing cost against environmental impact across the whole product life, not cost alone.

questions.q: A start-up finds that a product's manufacturing cost is higher than the price customers are willing to pay. What does this indicate about the design?
options: It is highly commercially viable
It is not commercially viable as currently designed
It has no environmental impact
It meets every user need
questions.explain: If it costs more to make than customers will pay, the product cannot be sold at a profit and is not commercially viable.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Design & Technology (J310) specification; Viability Of Design Solutions
